questions.question: Are Edmonton's garbage, green-bin and recycling collection schedules adequate for households?
questions.note: Collection calendars, capacity rules, waste audits and route records address the service levels and their household effects together.

claims.claim: Some Edmonton households, including households with five or more people, find one black bin every two weeks adequate.
Edmonton's standard residential black bins are collected every two weeks.
Edmonton collects residential green bins weekly.
Edmonton collects residential recycling or blue bags weekly.
Edmonton previously collected garbage weekly before changing to collection every two weeks.
Some residents report that their weekly green bins are only slightly filled or are not put out.
Black-bin garbage can rot or become especially bad during summer heat when collected every two weeks.
Some Edmonton households make one or two dump trips between biweekly garbage collections because the bin service is insufficient.
Diapers take substantial bin space, so families with two children in diapers produce more garbage.
Before garbage limits were introduced, some residents put out as many as 20 bags a week.
One resident uses weekly blue-bag collection to avoid running out of bin space.

questions.question: Can Edmonton households obtain waste carts that meet their household and medical needs?
questions.note: Cart-size, eligibility and accommodation policies, together with relevant account records, settle availability and household-specific decisions.

claims.claim: Edmonton residents can request or rent a larger or additional black bin from the City.
The City has granted larger garbage bins to residents with medical waste needs.
Edmonton changed the household-size threshold for a larger garbage bin from five people to seven.
The City took away a resident's larger bin after granting it for dialysis waste, saying the resident did not need it.
A five-person Edmonton household producing dialysis waste finds one garbage bin insufficient.
The City does not offer larger green bins on request.

questions.question: How much garbage can Edmonton residents take to an Eco Station for free?
questions.note: The same Eco Station disposal rules settle the differing daily and weekly allowance claims.

claims.claim: Edmonton residents can take up to two bags of garbage to an Eco Station per day for free.
Edmonton residents can take one extra bag of garbage per week to an eco centre.

questions.question: How does Edmonton charge households for waste service, and can residents opt out?
questions.note: Waste-service bylaws, rate schedules, utility bills and relevant account records cover the fee structure, cart charges and disputed charges.

claims.claim: Edmonton's waste collection fee is charged on Epcor utility bills rather than through property taxes.
Edmonton residents cannot cancel or opt out of garbage collection service.
At least one resident with the largest available garbage bin reported being billed $74 a month.
Edmonton residents are charged for waste disposal on their bills and again through property taxes.
A larger or additional garbage bin costs an extra $15 a month.
A resident was charged twice for extra garbage service after the City found garbage in the unit's bin.

questions.question: How reliable is Edmonton's waste collection, and what happens when a pickup is missed?
questions.note: Route logs, missed-collection complaints, 311 records and WasteWise schedules cover reported failures, remedies and successful pickups.

claims.claim: Edmonton residents can report a missed waste collection to the City or 311.
A missed garbage pickup can leave residents waiting another week even after they contact 311.
During one collection round, Edmonton crews collected green bins from part of an alley and skipped the rest.
At least one Edmonton resident's black bin is picked up before 8 a.m. every second Tuesday.
Edmonton's WasteWise app shows residents which waste streams are collected each week.
One Edmonton resident reports that the City has never missed their black-bin collection.

questions.question: What curbside waste rules does Edmonton enforce, and how are they enforced?
questions.note: Set-out rules, collection contracts and the City's waste-inspection program settle the cart-lid, extra-bag and sorting-enforcement claims.

claims.claim: GFL may leave a garbage bin uncollected as overloaded when its lid is open by half an inch.
Edmonton pays people to inspect residents' waste and check whether it is sorted correctly.
Edmonton garbage crews collect only what fits inside a black bin and may leave bags placed beside it.

questions.question: What waste service do Edmonton townhouse and condo residents receive?
questions.note: Multi-unit service standards and the affected complexes' collection records settle the cart numbers, sizes, streams and pickup schedules.

claims.claim: A development of about 20 Edmonton townhouses has three residential garbage bins and no large bin.
Some Edmonton condo or townhouse households receive small black bins that hold about two garbage bags.
At least one Edmonton townhouse complex has one large shared garbage bin collected weekly.
At least one Edmonton townhouse complex has separate compost and recycling bins beside its garbage bin.
Some Edmonton residents report that neighbours use garbage bins specifically labelled for another household.

questions.question: How much can Edmonton households reduce their garbage through recycling and composting?
questions.note: Waste audits and Edmonton's accepted-material rules measure both the divertible share and the effect of household sorting.

claims.claim: Recycling and composting can substantially reduce the amount of garbage an Edmonton household produces.
Some Edmonton households produce substantially more recycling and compost than garbage.
Most household waste in Edmonton is recyclable.
At least half of a typical household's garbage is recyclable.
About 95 percent of the things a typical household buys are recyclable.

questions.question: What happens to Edmonton's recycling and compost after collection?
questions.note: Accepted-material rules, facility-flow records and downstream contracts trace the listed recycling and compost outcomes.

claims.claim: Separate garbage and compost collection loads have been dumped onto the same pile.
Edmonton ships recyclable materials to Asia for processing.
If one item in an Edmonton recycling bag is dirty or does not belong, the entire bag is diverted to garbage.
Starting October 1, Edmonton is adding takeout containers, chip bags, snack wrappers, cereal bags and foam packaging to its recycling list.
Most material placed in Edmonton recycling ends up at the dump regardless of how residents sort it.
Edmonton's recyclable material is processed by waste management.
Edmonton has no designated recycling facility.
EWM uses different downstream processes for materials that appear to arrive together.
Some Edmonton residents assume items are recyclable based on container markings even when the local program does not accept them.
There are two dumps outside Edmonton.

questions.question: Has Edmonton's bin-based garbage system made the city cleaner or dirtier?
questions.note: Litter records and evaluations of the cart system's effect on exposed garbage settle both directions.

claims.claim: Edmonton has become dirtier since the new garbage system began.
Edmonton's bin system prevents garbage bags from being exposed for birds to tear open.

questions.question: Did Edmonton raise taxes when it reduced garbage collection to every two weeks?

claims.claim: Edmonton raised taxes when it reduced garbage collection from weekly to every two weeks.

questions.question: Does Edmonton plan to raise taxes substantially over the next four years?

claims.claim: Edmonton plans to raise taxes substantially over the next four years.

questions.question: Do Edmonton property taxes fund Ukraine?

claims.claim: Edmonton property taxes do not fund Ukraine.

questions.question: Is the City of Edmonton spending $14 million on an art gallery on 118 Avenue?

claims.claim: The City of Edmonton is spending $14 million on an art gallery on 118 Avenue.

questions.question: How is Edmonton spending public money on bike-lane construction?
questions.note: Bike-lane capital budgets and project construction records settle both general spending and the sidewalk example.

claims.claim: Edmonton spends tax dollars on bike lanes.
The City spent money removing sidewalks built the previous year to create bike lanes.

questions.question: Has Edmonton left hazardous sidewalks unreplaced despite decades of requests?
questions.note: Sidewalk condition assessments and the corresponding complaint and replacement records settle both assertions.

claims.claim: Some Edmonton asphalt sidewalks are hazardous and crumbling.
Residents have requested replacement sidewalks from the City for more than 40 years without success.

questions.question: Is Edmonton's parking enforcement fair and timely?
questions.note: Parking bylaws, enforcement case files and response-time logs cover the charge and delay claims.

claims.claim: The City charged a resident $500 for a vehicle parked on private property without prior warning.
Edmonton parking enforcement may take three days to respond to a report.

questions.question: Are Edmonton's tax-funded roads in poor condition?

claims.claim: Edmonton's roads are in poor condition despite being funded through taxes.

questions.question: What relationships do Edmonton's mayor and City Council have with infill developers?

claims.claim: Edmonton's City Council and mayor are connected to infill developers.

questions.question: Does Edmonton City Council give disproportionate attention to pro-bike advocates at daytime meetings?

claims.claim: Edmonton City Council mainly listens to pro-bike advocates who can attend daytime meetings while other residents are working.

questions.question: Who commutes by bicycle or other self-powered two-wheeled transportation in Edmonton?
questions.note: Commuting and employment data address both the existence of these commuters and whether they are working during the day.

claims.claim: Edmonton bike commuters are regular working people who work during the day.
Some Edmonton residents commute using self-powered two-wheeled transportation.
